title: A shorter link, a billion times
teaches: How to work out a system design on paper: defining requirements, estimating throughput and storage, specifying the API and data model, drawing the architecture, and generating short unique keys
summary: **Follow a structured sequence.** Define functional and non-functional requirements, estimate throughput and storage, specify the API and data model, and only then draw the architecture.
**State what is out of scope.** Explicitly excluding secondary subsystems such as click analytics and spam filtering keeps them from complicating the core architecture.

**Capacity estimates dictate the architecture.** Generating 100 million links a month produces 40 writes a second and 3 TB of data over five years: a single database handles the writes and storage, while the 4,000 to 10,000 reads a second require an in-memory cache.

**Optimise the schema for the dominant query.** A single table indexed by the short code as its primary key serves redirects with one lookup, matching a workload where reads outnumber writes a hundred to one.

**Random keys collide early due to the birthday problem.** Across N possible keys, the chance that any two keys match reaches 50% after roughly 1.2 √N draws, so a keyspace of 3.5 trillion seven-character codes has an even chance of at least one collision after just 2.2 million links.

**Allocate sequential IDs in blocks to avoid bottlenecks.** Assigning each application server a range of 1,000 counter values preserves collision-free generation while keeping the central counter off the critical write path.
**Truncated URL hashes still collide and require database checks.** Hashing the destination address also maps every user who shortens the same URL to a single shared record.

**HTTP 301 versus 302 trades server load against analytics.** A 301 permanent redirect lets browsers cache the destination and bypass the service on repeat clicks, saving bandwidth at the cost of visibility and control.

blocks.text: In 2002 a web developer, Kevin Gilbertson, was tired of long web addresses breaking across lines in newsgroup and email posts and no longer working when clicked. He wrote a small service that took a long address and returned a short one on his own domain, and called it TinyURL. Whenever anyone opened the short address, the service redirected their browser to the long one.

Once posts on Twitter were limited to 140 characters, short links were everywhere, and a service that began as one person's convenience was asked to hold billions of links and answer thousands of redirects a second, forever, since a short link that stops working breaks every page that used it.

In this lesson, we will design that service step by step, following the same order we will use for every system in the course. Before reading on, take a minute and sketch your own: what it must do, how big it gets, what you would store, and how you would generate the short codes. We will follow those exact steps, and each decision will shape the ones that follow.

parts.title: What it must do, and what it need not

blocks.text: Start with the functional requirements, in a few lines a user would recognise. Given a long URL, the service returns a short code. Given a short code, it redirects to the long URL, quickly and reliably. We should also let a user choose their own code (an alias) and set an expiry date on a link. Next, state explicitly what is out of scope for the initial design. Counting clicks by country and hour belongs in a separate analytics system that reads a log of redirects. Blocking users who shorten links to phishing pages is a large problem in its own right. Both matter, but neither should shape the core architecture.

Next, define the non-functional properties, which are where designs diverge. A redirect should add minimal latency to a user's request, say under 10 ms of processing time at the service on top of the network round trip. The redirect path requires high availability, because a failed lookup breaks the link for every reader of every page that embeds it. A code, once assigned, must never point anywhere else. Creating a link can tolerate higher latency and occasional failures, since a user can simply retry. This asymmetry between high-availability, low-latency reads and tolerant writes drives most of the architecture that follows.

parts.title: Before drawing any boxes, the numbers

blocks.text: Suppose the service creates 100 million new links a month. Using the approximations from lesson 1, a month is about 2.6 million seconds, which gives an average write throughput of about 40 new links a second, and perhaps 200 writes a second at peak. Short links are read far more often than they are created; if we assume a 100-to-1 read-to-write ratio, the service handles about 4,000 redirects a second on average, and we should provision for 10,000 redirects a second at peak.

For storage, 100 million links a month over five years is 6 billion links. Each row holds the short code, the long URL (a couple of hundred bytes on average), an owner ID and two timestamps; including database index overhead, estimate 500 bytes per row. Six billion rows at 500 bytes is 3 TB. That fits on a single server's flash drives with room to spare, and 40 writes a second is a light load for any relational database. These estimates immediately rule out unnecessary complexity: we do not need to partition data across multiple machines on day one. Instead, we must design for the read throughput of 10,000 queries a second, which exceeds the 3,000 queries a second this course assumes a single database server can handle (a benchmark we will also use in lesson 4), and for high availability on the redirect path.

Next, we define the **API**: the requests external clients can make and the exact data sent over the network for each. Two endpoints are enough. Creating a link is an HTTP POST containing the long URL (and an optional custom alias) that returns the short code. Following a link is an HTTP GET requesting the code path itself, which returns an HTTP redirect response carrying the long URL in its `Location` header. Specifying the API early forces concrete decisions that high-level diagrams gloss over, such as the format of a code, the error returned when an alias is already taken, and which HTTP status code the redirect uses.

blocks.caption: The two API calls and the single database table behind them. Every redirect requires one lookup by primary key.

blocks.text: Next, we design the data model. List the queries the system must run and their frequencies, and optimise the schema for the most common operation. Here, redirects outnumber link creations a hundred to one, and each redirect fetches a single row by its short code. A single table with the short code as its **primary key** (the column the database enforces as unique and indexes each row by) answers every redirect with one index lookup. Nothing in the initial design requires a join, a secondary index search or a table scan.

Choosing the HTTP redirect status code involves a trade-off between server load and analytics. HTTP **301** indicates a permanent move, allowing browsers to cache the response and go straight to the long URL on subsequent clicks without contacting the shortener. That reduces server load and saves the user a network round trip, but the service never sees those repeat clicks and can never update the destination URL. HTTP **302** indicates a temporary move, instructing the browser to request the short URL on every click so the service can log traffic and disable links that turn out to be malicious. A service that relies on click analytics uses 302 and provisions for the extra read throughput.[^redirect]

The hardest part of the design is assigning every new link a short code that no other link uses. Using the 62 alphanumeric characters (`a` to `z`, `A` to `Z` and `0` to `9`), a seven-character string yields 62⁷ possible codes, or about 3.5 trillion. Six billion links consume less than 0.2% of this keyspace. The simplest approach is to pick seven characters at random for each new link. To see if that works, we need to calculate how soon two links will randomly pick the same code.

blocks.caption: The probability of at least one collision among randomly chosen codes, plotted against the number of codes generated. Change the alphabet size and code length to see how the curve shifts.
blocks.task: Estimate how many random codes we can generate before the chance of any collision among them reaches 50%.

blocks.text: It takes about 2.2 million codes. This is the **birthday problem**: in a room of 23 people there is a 50% chance that two share a birthday, even though there are 365 days in a year, because collision probability depends on the number of pairs, and 23 people form 253 pairs. Across N possible codes, the chance that any two of them match reaches 50% after about 1.2 √N codes; √(3.5 trillion) is 1.87 million, giving roughly 2.2 million codes. In general, n random selections produce about n² / 2N collisions, so across 6 billion links a purely random scheme would generate (6 × 10⁹)² / (7 × 10¹²), or about 5.1 million collisions. Therefore, we must check every random code before returning it: insert the new row only if that primary key does not already exist, and generate a fresh random code if it does. Because the database enforces uniqueness on the primary key during insertion, and because the keyspace is 99.8% empty, a collision retry is rarely needed. Random generation with database retries is simple and works well.

Alternatively, a sequential **counter** never collides: assign link 1 the code for 1, link 2 the code for 2, and so on, encoding each integer in base 62.[^base62] However, if every create request must query a single counter, that machine becomes both a throughput bottleneck and a single point of failure for all writes. Flickr faced this exact problem when generating photo IDs and published its solution in 2010: two small MySQL instances called **ticket servers**, one configured to issue odd numbers and the other even numbers, so either machine could fail without halting uploads.[^tickets] We can remove the counter from the critical write path entirely by having each application server request a block of 1,000 numbers at a time and assign them from memory. If the counter service goes offline for a minute, the application servers continue issuing codes from their local blocks. If an application server crashes, it loses the unused numbers in its current block, which wastes negligible capacity in a keyspace of 3.5 trillion. To ensure the counter service never issues the same block twice after a reboot, it writes the upper bound of each allocated block to disk before returning the range to the application server.

Sequential counters have one drawback: the resulting codes are predictable. An attacker can step through `aZ3kQ9w`, `aZ3kQ9x`, `aZ3kQ9y` and scrape every link in the database, including URLs that users assumed were unlisted. Permuting the integers before encoding them hides the sequence while preserving uniqueness: if we multiply each counter value by a properly chosen constant modulo 62⁷, every integer still maps to a unique code, but consecutive numbers scatter widely across the keyspace. Because this mathematical permutation is reversible, two different counter values can never produce the same code.[^shuffle]

A common flawed approach is to hash the long URL (using MD5 or SHA-256) and take the first seven characters of the output. Because a truncated hash behaves like a random string of the same length, it still reaches a 50% chance of at least one collision after 2.2 million links and still requires a database uniqueness check and retry loop on insert. Worse, hashing the URL assigns the exact same code to every user who shortens the same address. While deduplicating identical URLs saves storage, it causes separate users to share one link record, colliding on custom expiry times and individual click counts. Whichever generation scheme we choose, we must uphold our initial requirement that an assigned code never changes its destination.

With the scale, API, schema and key generation settled, we can draw the system architecture. A **load balancer** distributes incoming traffic across several **stateless** application servers (servers that store no client state locally between requests, allowing any instance to handle any call and to be replaced if it fails). Behind the application servers sits the relational database holding the links table. In front of the database sits an in-memory **cache** that stores recently requested mappings so that most redirects are served from RAM without querying the disk. Link traffic follows a skewed distribution: a small fraction of newly shared links receives the vast majority of clicks, while older links are rarely accessed. To size the cache, estimate how many unique links account for most of a day's traffic. If 20 million active links generate 95% of daily redirects, caching 20 million rows at 500 bytes each requires 10 GB of RAM, which fits easily on a single cache server. We will cover caching strategies in detail in lesson 5; here, a single cache layer reduces database read load by an order of magnitude.

blocks.caption: The complete architecture. Redirects read from the cache first; link creations write to the database, and periodically an application server fetches a fresh block of IDs from the key service (shown here every 20th write for visibility; in production, every 1,000 writes). Click an application server to simulate a crash and watch the load balancer route traffic around it.
blocks.task: Observe the redirect request flow, then switch the view to link creation.

blocks.text: The read and write paths are largely decoupled. A redirect hits the load balancer, an application server and usually only the cache; the 5% to 10% of requests that miss the cache also query the database, and in lesson 4 we will add read replicas so redirects can survive a primary database failure. Creating a new link hits an application server, writes to the database, and every thousandth time requests a block from the key service. The latency-sensitive, high-availability redirect path never communicates with the key service, leaving all state coordination on the write path where higher latency is acceptable. This separation follows directly from the non-functional requirements we established at the start.

As traffic grows, we can scale each component independently. If read throughput increases tenfold, we add database read replicas to share the cache-miss traffic, a pattern we will examine along with replication lag in lesson 4. If the cache server fails, all 10,000 reads a second hit the database simultaneously, causing a cascading failure that we will address in lessons 5 and 15. If we deploy application servers across multiple continents to reduce write latency, each region can pull its own distinct blocks of IDs. None of that complexity is needed in the initial deployment.

blocks.title: The method
points: Define functional requirements, out-of-scope features, and non-functional requirements (latency, availability, immutability).
Estimate scale: average and peak request throughput, and total storage over several years.
Specify the API: each endpoint and its exact request and response payloads.
Design the data model: index the schema around the highest-throughput query.
The boxes, then the part that is hard.

blocks.caption: Six questions on working a design out
blocks.task: Choose the best answer to each

items.ask: A link shortener creates 100 million links a month and retains them for five years at about 500 bytes per record. What does this capacity estimate tell us about the initial database architecture?
choices: The table must be sharded across many database servers from day one, because billions of rows cannot fit on a single machine
About 3 TB of storage and 40 writes a second fit on one database server; read throughput is the bottleneck that requires caching
Storage cannot be estimated until the click analytics pipeline is designed, since click logs determine the row size
items.why: Six billion rows at 500 bytes is 3 TB, and 40 writes a second is a light write load for a single machine. The 4,000 to 10,000 redirects a second are the bottleneck we must design for, using an in-memory cache and database read replicas.

items.ask: Seven-character codes drawn from a 62-character alphabet provide about 3.5 trillion unique possibilities. If each new link is assigned a random code without checking existing rows, roughly how many links can be created before the probability of any collision among them reaches 50%?
items.why: By the birthday problem, the chance of at least one collision among all codes reaches 50% after about 1.2 times the square root of the keyspace size, and 1.2 × 1.87 million is roughly 2.2 million codes.

items.ask: Which method of generating short codes guarantees zero collisions without querying a central service on every write request?
choices: Take the first seven characters of an MD5 hash of the long URL
Query a single counter database for the next sequential integer on every link creation
Allocate distinct blocks of sequential integers to each application server to assign from memory
items.why: Allocating ranges in blocks preserves the counter's uniqueness guarantee while reducing calls to the central coordinator to once every 1,000 writes, allowing application servers to tolerate brief coordinator outages. A truncated hash still collides, and querying a single counter on every write creates a bottleneck and single point of failure.

items.ask: Why does a link-shortening service that provides click analytics return HTTP 302 rather than HTTP 301?
choices: Because a 302 allows browsers to cache the redirect locally, reducing page load latency for users
Because browsers cache a 301 response and go directly to the destination URL on repeat visits, bypassing the shortener
Because an HTTP 301 response limits the `Location` header to 255 bytes
items.why: HTTP 301 indicates a permanent redirect, which browsers cache. Caching reduces server load, but subsequent clicks from the same browser never reach the shortener, preventing it from counting repeat visits or updating the destination URL.

items.ask: In the completed architecture, why is the key generation service excluded from the redirect path?
choices: Redirects only look up existing records, and isolating the high-availability read path from write-side dependencies reduces points of failure
The key service takes hundreds of milliseconds to respond, which would violate the 10 ms redirect latency budget
The key service stores generated codes only in volatile memory and does not record the destination URLs
items.why: Our requirements specified that redirects need high availability whereas link creation can tolerate occasional delays. Keeping key allocation strictly on the write path ensures that an outage in the key service never breaks an existing short link.

items.ask: We estimated storage capacity and request throughput before drawing the system architecture. How did those calculations shape the design?
choices: They showed that 3 TB and 40 writes a second fit on a single database, focusing our architecture on caching the 10,000 reads a second
They had no structural effect, as the components would be identical and the estimates only verify hardware sizing afterwards
They determined that the short codes must be exactly seven characters long
items.why: Because 3 TB of data and 40 writes a second fit comfortably on one machine, we avoided premature database sharding and focused on serving 10,000 redirects a second with an in-memory cache. Designing the architecture without estimating scale first often leads to unnecessary partitioning. The seven-character code length came from collision math over 6 billion links, not from the throughput order.

base62.title: Base 62
base62.text: Encoding an integer in base 62 works like base 10, using 62 symbols (`0` to `9`, `a` to `z`, and `A` to `Z`) instead of ten digits. Representing 3.5 trillion requires seven base-62 characters, whereas six characters cover up to 62⁶ (about 56.8 billion), so an unpadded sequential counter produces codes of six characters or fewer for the first 56.8 billion links.

redirect.title: Two newer codes
redirect.text: HTTP later added 307 and 308, which behave like 302 and 301 but promise that the browser repeats the same method (a POST stays a POST). For a GET of a short link they make no difference, and most shorteners still use 301 or 302.

tickets.title: Flickr's ticket servers
tickets.text: Each Flickr ticket server was a dedicated MySQL instance holding a single-row table with an `AUTO_INCREMENT` primary key. To request a new ID, an application server executed a `REPLACE INTO` statement on that row and called `LAST_INSERT_ID()`. One server was configured with an offset to issue odd integers (1, 3, 5) and the other even integers (2, 4, 6), allowing application servers to alternate between them or fall back to one if the other failed.

shuffle.title: Hiding a counter
shuffle.text: For modular multiplication to permute the keyspace without collisions, the multiplier must be coprime to 62⁷ (meaning it shares no prime factors with 62, so it cannot be divisible by 2 or 31). That guarantees a one-to-one mapping across all 62⁷ values in a pseudo-random order. Because a determined observer can still recover a linear multiplier from a few sequential outputs, production systems often use a format-preserving block cipher (such as a Feistel network), which encrypts a 42-bit integer into another 42-bit integer under a secret key. Because decryption is deterministic, the cipher is guaranteed never to map two different counter values to the same output.
